ca_northwest_chute: From Tower Lake climb gravel, talus and grass south to Tower Pass, where the peak comes into view, and cross the basin beyond. Go up slabs beside a lingering snow patch to the northwest ridge, then leave the ridge onto its west side and traverse into the Northwest Chute, scrambling class 3 up it to the summit, about 2,250 ft above the lake.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard: From camp, go cross-country around Upper Chain Lake and climb the couloir above it: steep heather, mossy slabs and brush low down, then huge white talus higher up, to a notch between two points on the crest. Take the right-hand, southern point, working around the right (east) side of the summit block to a short, exposed Class 3 step and mantle onto the top.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_: Above the step, angle steadily up and south on a well-cairned path through open forest and hillside, about an hour, to the col.
Drop just over the col into the flats below, where the boulder camp has low-impact sites on rock and gravel among the boulders. There is no reliable water here; carry it up from the lake.
wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge: From the lake, follow the trail around the west shore to the south end, cross the talus beyond the campsites and pick up the climbers' path along the Colchuck Glacier moraine until the northwest face opens up. Backbone starts about 200 ft left of Serpentine Arete on bushy, left-trending ramps; scramble up and left, then back right to a slung tree and terrace, and climb the ridge, the offwidth and the Fin to the summit.
Descend the east ledges and the sandy summit gully toward Aasgard Pass. Late in the season the upper gully can be icy, and parties rappel on rock anchors to avoid the ice slope.
wa_dragontail_peak_r2: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed junction and turn left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, cross Mountaineer Creek and climb the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft. Continue along the west shore toward the south end for the camps. In winter and spring expect snowshoes or skis and avalanche exposure.
From the south end of the lake, work up talus and snow onto the crest of the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine below the north face.

Follow the moraine toward the face and cross the apron to its lowest point, where the snow runs highest into the rock; the start is the snow ramps just right of that toe. Move as a rope team across the apron, which sits under rock and icefall.

Climb about 800 ft of low-angle snow and ice, then belayed runnels connecting the snow bands right of center, through a constriction between rock bands, to the band of dark rock two-thirds of the way up the face.

Follow the ice runnels splitting the dark band and the thin M4 mixed crux, continue up sustained ice above it, then traverse into the third of the Triple Couloirs and climb it. From its top, a short snow scramble up and right leads to the summit.
wa_dragontail_peak_serpentine_arete: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed junction and turn left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, cross Mountaineer Creek and grind up the rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft.

Go around the lake's west shore to its south end, boulder-hop onto the crest of the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine and follow it south toward the northwest face to the band of orange rock low on the wall. Cross the moat onto 4th-class ledges through the orange band, then climb the arete's crack and dihedral pitches and the ridge crest and sandy gully to the summit.
Head down the loose sandy gully shared with the top of Backbone Ridge, downclimb or boot-ski the upper Snow Creek Glacier snowfield where it remains, then traverse east to Aasgard Pass.
wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge: Take the Buck Creek Trail 1.4 miles, bear right on the Chiwawa River Trail #1550, stay left at the Red Mountain junction near 5 miles and ford the river. Climb open forest cross-country to a basin near 5,500 ft and a bench near 6,300 ft, then traverse up to the 7,200 ft Chiwawa-Fortress col. From the col a loose class 3-4 gully gains the East Ridge; follow the crest past a chimney step to the summit.
wa_massie_peak_west_route: From Massie Lake follow the faint high-route tread northwest toward Pass No Pass for roughly 1.5 miles, then leave it and turn uphill, climber's right, over heather benches and talus onto Massie Peak's broad west ridge, near a shoulder at about 6,420 ft.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route: Climb Smithbrook Trail #1590 through brush and an old boulder field into forest, entering the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness within the first half mile, and switchback about 1.2 miles to Union Gap, where it meets the Pacific Crest Trail.

Turn left (south) on the PCT and follow its gentle, rolling grade about 1.4 miles to an unnamed gap near 5,100 ft. The unsigned climbers' path leaves uphill on the right, marked only by a single white rock, just before the trail starts dropping toward Lake Valhalla; if the lake is in view or the trail is losing height, you have gone past.

Stay on the main path that heads for the summit as it climbs through heather onto the crest. The crest flattens into an alpine garden; the first high point is not the top, so drop briefly to a small saddle and climb to the rocky true summit.
wa_mount_stuart_cascadian_couloir: Walk the old road from the trailhead about 0.3 mile to the fork and bear right onto the Ingalls Way Trail, leaving the Esmeralda Basin Trail.

Climb the Ingalls Way Trail to the signed Longs Pass junction near 5,440 ft and turn right, then switchback up the open, shadeless hillside to the pass, where Mount Stuart and the Cascadian Couloir first come into view. Start before dawn in summer.

Descend the steep, loose trail down the north side of the pass, losing about 1,300 ft to Ingalls Creek, and cross the creek on the log to meet the Ingalls Creek Trail on the far bank. The slope can hold firm snow early in the season.

Turn right (east, downstream) on the Ingalls Creek Trail and follow it a short way to an unmarked climbers' path on the left. Take it north through the meadow and camps to the toe of the couloir. Fill water here; none is reliable higher up.
wa_mount_stuart_ice_cliff_glacier: Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs and follow the unmaintained climbers' path upstream, staying low beside the creek with the creek on your left rather than following cairns up and right into the boulder slope near 4,675 ft. After about 1.5 miles, where the valley steepens, turn right (west) and climb talus and forest into the flat hanging basin near 5,400 ft beneath the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers.
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake junction and stay right toward Stuart Lake. Where the trail later turns uphill and starts switchbacking away from Mountaineer Creek, leave it, cross the creek and follow the climbers' path up the valley, then climb loose talus into the basin under the Sherpa Glacier. Angle up the moraine to the lowest rock of the North Ridge at about 6,600 ft, with the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left.
wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir: Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs and follow the unmaintained climbers' path upstream, staying low beside the creek rather than following cairns up and right into the boulder slope near 4,675 ft. After about 1.5 miles, where the valley steepens, turn right (west) and climb the steep talus and forest slope into the small flat basin near 5,400 ft beneath the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers.
wa_mount_stuart_west_ridge: Aim for the deep middle gully of the three parallel gullies on the lower ridge, the one with a house-sized boulder at its foot. Push through scrub into it and scramble sandy class 3 granite up and rightward, with short class 4 steps, to the notch at its head where Long John Tower stands directly ahead. Snow can linger in the gully into midsummer and is often icy early in the day.
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the junction and turn left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, crossing Mountaineer Creek and switchbacking up to the north end of Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft.

Follow the trail along the west shore of Colchuck Lake to the boulder field at its south end, then climb Aasgard Pass, roughly 2,200 ft in a little over a mile of steep, loose scree and dirt. Under lingering snow into early July a creek runs hidden beneath the talus, and rockfall from parties above is common.

From Gnome Tarn traverse northeast over slabs and talus to the base of the south face at about 7,350 ft. The route starts in a crack system on white granite just left of two deep chimneys, below a small stand of scrubby pines about a pitch up.

Climb the wide crack and low fifth-class ground to the trees, then a crack exiting right on knobs to the highest trees, then sustained gully climbing to a belay below the obvious chockstone. Steep double cracks lead into the tunnel behind it.

Squirm through the hole behind the chockstone and work right into the flaring 5.9+ squeeze chimney, the crux, and belay on the ledge above. The final pitch stems a sustained left-facing corner on knobs straight to the summit.

Walk east from the summit to the slung anchors and rappel the north face: about four single-rope rappels of 25 to 30 m off blocks and chockstones, then a 3rd-class downclimb, or one or two more rappels right of the gully in its place. Bring extra tat to back up old webbing.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble: Cross the creek on a downed log at the confluence and leave the maintained tread. Follow the South Fork drainage upward, staying roughly 50 ft above the water to avoid the worst alder and log-hopping, for about 2 miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder and downed timber on a boot path that comes and goes. The timber thins around 5,600 ft and a ravine opens into the talus and scree basin below the southeast face.
wa_sherpa_glacier: From the col, follow the ridge west over simple Class 3 blocks, taking some ground just on the south side of the crest. The ridge passes above the head of the Cascadian Couloir to the false summit, then continues a short way to the true summit. Note the col carefully in wind or poor visibility so the glacier descent can be found again.
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge: Hike the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) along Mountaineer Creek, staying right toward Lake Stuart at the Colchuck Lake junction. About 3.5 to 4 miles in, before the lake, leave the trail, cross Mountaineer Creek and follow a boot path over talus benches west of the creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin. Climb talus west-northwest to a deep gully and the notch at about 7,000 ft, then climb the North Ridge, staying just east of the crest, to the summit.
wa_south_face_12: At about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391, not the Bean Creek fork, and follow it up Beverly Creek. At about 2.8 miles the Fourth Creek Trail (#1218) leaves at a faint fork in a grove of trees.
Turn right onto the Fourth Creek Trail (#1218) and make the steep 0.3-mile push to the low, treed crest of Fourth Creek Pass, where Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail first come into view.

Descend the Fourth Creek Trail north down the far side of the pass into the Fourth Creek drainage, about 3.5 miles, to Ingalls Creek at about 4,200 ft. Ford the creek by wading or on a footlog; it runs cold and swift early in the season and can be iced in the shoulders.
Once across Ingalls Creek, walk a short way to the flat camping at the Fourth Creek confluence beside the Ingalls Creek Trail.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme: Take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft. From Goat Pass, traverse onto and across the Stuart Glacier, watching for crevasses, to a fourth-class gully that climbs to the obvious notch in the North Ridge at about 8,200 ft.

From the notch, stay on the east side and take an easy ramp to the crest, then follow roughly eleven pitches of exposed low- to mid-fifth-class granite to the Great Gendarme. Climb its 5.8-5.9 dihedral and offwidth, traverse right back to the crest at a small saddle, and finish with about three pitches of blocky, lower-angle ground to the summit.
wa_bears_breast_mountain_southwest_face: From I-90 Exit 34, go north on 468th Ave SE about 0.6 mile and turn right onto the Middle Fork Road (FS Road 56). Follow it about 12 miles as the pavement gives out, pass the Middle Fork Trailhead, and bear right onto the rough road signed for Dingford and Dutch Miller Gap. Drive about 5 to 6 more rough miles, high clearance recommended, to the gate at the Dingford Creek Trailhead at about 1,500 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge: Walk or bike the closed road east up the Middle Fork about 7.7 miles to Hardscrabble Horse Camp, where bikes must stop. Head upstream toward Hardscrabble Creek and ford the Middle Fork, which can run cold and thigh-deep in July (the nearest bridge is at Pedro Camp). From the south bank go cross-country up steep forest and brush on the north ridge to its steep granite, then three class 5 leads along a knife-edge crest and three class 3-4 leads to the summit.
wa_chimney_rock_east_face_direct: Take Pete Lake Trail 1323 up the Cooper River past Pete Lake to the PCT, then about a mile of PCT to the hairpin in an old avalanche swath near 3,360 ft. The Chimney Creek climbers' path leaves the forest right of the twin waterfalls to the west and climbs to camp below the moraine, about 4,700 ft. Drop to the lower Chimney Glacier, rope up, gain the upper glacier by the gully left of the icefall, and climb to the moat beneath the main summit.

Cross the moat onto rock and climb one pitch to a broad heather ledge system. From its right side, follow a leftward-sloping ledge system through faces and gullies to the right end of Key Ledge, about two-thirds of the way up the face and a common bivy, then climb three more pitches to the main summit.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route: Hike north on the Pacific Crest Trail, climbing switchbacks to the exposed ledge of Kendall Katwalk at about 5 miles, then continue north past Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake and around the flanks of Alaska Mountain to where the trail runs a few hundred feet above Joe Lake, about 9 miles from the pass.
Leave the PCT at a flowery meadow northeast of Joe Lake and climb a talus slope into the basin below the west face, which is in plain view from the meadow.

From the basin, climb left of a wide, loose chimney to the top of the ridge, follow the ridge to a belay ledge, then take a ramp and two short dihedrals on loose, lichen-covered rock to the summit, about four pitches to 5.6.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route: Climb Dingford Creek Trail 1005 past Pumpkinseed Falls and several stream crossings to the fork at about 3 miles, bear right on the Hester Lake Trail, and gain about 1,000 ft in 2.5 miles to Hester Lake. Continue to Little Hester Lake and climb the boulder field directly south of it to Price's east ridge, east of the 5,440-ft subpeak. Traverse the steep north side of the ridge to the 5,400-ft col just east of the summit, then scramble the final ridge to the top.
wa_mount_si_haystack_scramble: Hike the Mount Si Trail about 4 miles and 3,150 ft past Snag Flats to the meadow of Haystack Basin at about 3,900 ft, then follow the path northeast to the wooden bench at the base of the Haystack. Scramble the rocky northeast-facing gully to the saddle between the main and north summits, then turn south over two exposed class 3 steps of slabby rock to the small summit.
wa_northwest_face_4: From I-90 Exit 34, go north on 468th Ave SE and turn right on the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FS Road 56). Follow it about 12 miles to the large Middle Fork trailhead on the right, continue past it, and turn right onto the gravel road just after a large concrete bridge. Drive about 6 heavily potholed miles to the gate at the Dingford Creek Trailhead, about 1,430 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route: Cross US 2 on foot from the pullout and pick up the old Yodelin ski-area road, which leaves the highway shoulder into second-growth timber.
Follow the old road to its end, then head west into the woods up the Nason Creek valley, staying near the creek.
Continue west up the valley, crossing Nason Creek on a snow bridge or log where it is most reliable, into the open basin between Tye Peak and the Spinnaker-Martin ridge at about 4,600 ft.
wa_beckey_tate: From the pullout, walk south into the trees to pick up the cairned climbers' trail and follow it along the west side of Early Winters Creek for about half a mile, to where the West Face line crosses the creek at the edge of the talus field. For this route, do not cross here.
wa_black_peak_east_buttress: From Wing Lake, climb the easy lower portion of the East Buttress above the east side of the basin, then follow the gully system above it through a series of Class 3 and 4 steps on fairly solid rock to the summit.
wa_colfax_peak_polish_route: Follow the Heliotrope Ridge Trail (#677) about 2 miles up through forest, crossing several creeks and passing the old Kulshan Cabin site, to the fork where the hiker trail heads left toward Heliotrope Creek and the climbers' path branches right.
Take the right fork and climb steeply, about 1,000 ft in a mile, up the crest of the Hogsback moraine to the bivy sites at around 6,000 ft at the edge of the Coleman Glacier.

Rope up and join the standard Coleman Glacier boot track, then bear climber's right off it toward the bench beneath Colfax's north face, watching for crevasses and for serac fall from the icefall above.

From the bench, gear up and go to the bergschrund below the obvious continuous ice line in the middle of the face, just left of the Cosley-Houston gully. It is often large and overhanging; parties have had to traverse in from the right on mixed ground and tunnel through overhanging snow to reach the ice.
Above the bergschrund the ice stands up immediately: the first pitch is a full ropelength of sustained steep ice leading to a snow slope below the crux band.
Cross the short snow slope above the first ice pitch to the base of the crux band, where the hanging curtain forms.

Climb the dagger pitch, then a couple more steep ice steps in the right-hand gully to the upper snowfield, which cuts between rock buttresses and trends up and right to the top of the face; a short traverse and scramble reaches the summit.
wa_complete_south_buttress: From the pullout, follow the cairned climbers' track down through timber, across State Creek (the last reliable water), and up into the meadows and boulder field below the peak to about 6,500 ft. Where the standard South Buttress track bears right toward its entry gully, leave the path and contour southeast on talus and heather benches, off-trail, to the very bottom of the ridge, where easy ledgy slabs mark its toe.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge: Cross the river on logs and climb the steep climbers' path beside Eldorado Creek, then the boulder fields and the Eldorado Glacier to the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak and the high camps near 7,400 ft, roughly 4 miles and 6,000 ft of gain. From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to the col between Point 8386 and Dorado Needle, about 7,600 ft.

Climb straight off the col on loose, thin first-pitch rock (a slung horn sits about 100 ft up), then several ropelengths along the ridge. Drop into a notch, traverse the glacier to a ledge with pale quartzite bands (watch the moat) and regain the ridge to the sub-summit tower. Two short rappels reach the notch below the summit, then two 5.7 crack pitches lead to the top.
wa_forbidden_peak_northwest_face: From the top of the snow and ice, solo or simul-climb about 500 ft of steep, somewhat loose 4th to low-5th class rock up the rib, keeping the party close to limit rockfall, to where it narrows into the knife-edge.

Cross the exposed knife-edge on the crest at 5.6 and continue straight into the 5.8 crux on solid granite flakes and cracks. Where the rib blends into the face, head up and left into a wide chimney, then follow low-5th to 5.6 cracks and flakes on good rock to the summit.
wa_himmelhorn_wild_hair_crack: From the Goodell Creek trailhead, about 600 ft, take the Stump Hollow approach and cross into Crescent Creek Basin, with good bivy sites below Mount Terror. From the basin climb the narrow gully to the Himmelhorn-Ottohorn col, snow early in the season and icy snow and moats later, then scramble about 50 ft east of the col to where the rock turns near vertical.

Climb the twin cracks, the right-hand one preferred, then the signature vertical crack, sparsely protected for its first 20 ft. Easy scrambling leads to a notch just below the false summit, then an exposed ridge with airy low-5th moves reaches the summit block.
wa_last_chance_for_gas_aka_tricky_start: The cliff is a few feet from the pullout, on the left side of the road. Find the wall's one continuous crack, often with a fixed rope hanging in it; this route is the line immediately to its right.

Climb the pumpy, technical first 10 ft, the crux of the route, then easier ground to the anchor. The bolts are old, so most parties walk around to the top of the cliff and rig a top-rope from above instead of leading.
wa_liberty_bell_independence_route: From the pond, round its east end and follow the cairned climbers' path into the forest for about an hour to the talus below the East Face. Walk right along the base, past the Liberty Crack starts, to the far right-hand end of the face below the red Baer Ceiling roof, then climb the lower pitches of horizontal breaks, cracks and a quartz corner to the alcove below the ceiling.

Continue up the thin cracks past the stacked ceilings and the crux corner beneath the Well Hung Ceiling to M&M Ledge, then up chimneys and the 2-3 inch splitter to the anchor below the Hercan Roofs. A slab traverse up and right gains the ridge crest, and 3rd-class scrambling leads to the summit.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route: From camp, cross the basin to the north and northeast over talus and scree, staying on the McMillan side of the basin rather than crossing the Barrier, to the foot of the southwest arete; expect snow and moats at the base well into summer. Climb the lower arete on class 4 and low fifth-class rock, testing every hold, to the fractured band below the summit block.
Continue up the arete above the loose band on class 4 and low fifth-class rock to the summit.
wa_mount_ann_scramble: From the saddle, take the boot path southwest and then south along the ridge crest to about 5,300 ft, where the ridge steepens and the path becomes hard to follow.
Follow cairns up through the steeper section until the crest re-forms, then along it to the tree-covered top of Peak 5681. It is not the summit; the ridge continues west.
Scramble about half a mile west along the up-and-down ridge crest, steeper than it looks on the map, to the summit; the final bit is class 2-3.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble: From camp, head south up toward Buckindy's north side to the toe of the glacier and rope up.
Climb the glacier roped, weaving between crevasses while the snow is still firm, to the band of open crevasses and moat below the summit rocks.
Get across the moat onto the rock and scramble Class 4 up the north slopes to the summit.
wa_mount_chaval_scramble: Above the cliff band the route breaks out onto open west-facing slopes. Climb northeast across the basin and up a steep gully to the pass in the ridge at about 5,920 ft, cross to the north side of the ridge, and traverse east until the broad west face and its single left-to-right diagonal ramp are in front of you.

Climb the diagonal ramp, on snow or on the heather-and-rock band to its left, from left to right to the summit ridge, then turn left and scramble to the top. The heather and moss on the ramp make it insecure, and it is harder facing out on the way down.
wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route: From Perfect Pass, stay on the west side of the range and head south off trail on snow, talus and heather: across the edge of the Challenger Glacier, below Crooked Thumb and Ghost Peak, and along under the west side of Phantom Peak. Keep going south to the col between Phantom and Crowder, the low point of the ridge running south from Phantom at a little over 6,000 ft.
wa_mount_despair_east_route: Follow the Thornton Lakes Trail on the old roadbed, nearly flat for about a mile, to the crossing of Thornton Creek, the last easy water. Leave the trail there and bushwhack upslope; small cliff bands force a leftward, northerly traverse through slide alder to a hanging meadow around 3,800 ft.

Climb the ferny talus slope above the meadow, then push about 1,000 ft up steep timber through cedar limbs and heavy brush to a rocky shoulder on Thornton Ridge at about 5,300 ft. Parties have been cliffed out on this stretch and had to backtrack.
From the shoulder, traverse north over rock and heather, working around minor obstacles, to the flat benches near Thornton Pass at about 6,050 ft, the standard camp.

From camp, drop back to about 5,300 ft and cross shoulder-high brush to a cascading stream with open bedrock slabs. Downclimb the slabs about 200 ft, drop through forest and steep duff to about 4,600 ft, then traverse into the open basin below Triumph Pass and climb to the pass at about 5,500 ft.
Descend the north-facing snowfield below the pass to Lake Regret, often still partly frozen. Skirt it on the west-side moraine rather than crossing the ice.
From Lake Regret, re-climb to about 5,300 ft and traverse north across heather benches, slabs and shallow ravines to Upper Despair Lake.

From the lake, climb the heathery ridge to its east, then talus and snow, to the cliff band directly below the southeast face. Pass the band and climb the rock above to the summit; expect short roped steps on loose, mossy granite, with no fixed anchors anywhere on the peak.
wa_mount_goode_northeast_buttress: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound, losing height steadily along Bridge Creek, for about 10 miles to the junction with the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail near North Fork Camp.

Turn onto the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail and head upstream; it grows brushier and less maintained, with a log crossing at Grizzly Creek. Where the tread fades around mile 13 to 14, ford the North Fork a few steps upstream at a cairn, climb scree and third-class slabs on climber's right of the big waterfall draining the Goode Glacier, and follow the alder tunnel through the slide alder to camp near the glacier toe.

Cross the Goode Glacier, watching for crevasses and serac fall, to the band of red ledges at the toe of the buttress, and get across the moat there. One or two low fifth-class pitches on loose blocks trend right to the crest; follow over 1,000 ft of 3rd and 4th class, step right around a short unprotectable 5.7 slab near 8,000 ft, then climb about five pitches of 5.4 to 5.5 easing to the summit.

From the summit, make three rappels down along the ridge to Black Tooth Notch. The first runs nearly straight down the ridgeline; the second and third traverse to rappeller's left, so watch the rope tails for snags. Anchors are slung horns and blocks, and a single 60 m rope reaches every station.

From the notch, cross the exposed 4th-class ledge, then make about three more single-rope rappels into the Southwest Couloir and downclimb class 3 below them. Where the gully narrows into cliffs lower down, exit left onto easier ground rather than rappelling the waterfall band.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier: Walk around the gate and follow the old road past the lodge site about a mile to its end at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, drop northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley to the toe of the White Salmon Glacier and climb glacier and moraine to a bivy at the rock outcrops on its eastern edge. Then traverse climber's left beneath the upper ice to the foot of the Hanging Glacier, staying right of the North Face's avalanche paths.

Climb the Hanging Glacier on roped glacier ground and ice steps up to about 65 degrees, outflanking a large crevasse high up; serac fall is a real hazard. Its top joins the Crystal Glacier, which leads onto the upper plateau beside the summit pyramid. Finish up the pyramid's east ridge, roped rock at about 5.3 to 5.6, to the summit.
wa_mount_shuksan_north_face: Continue up the White Salmon valley toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier, then climb to the shoulder at about 5,500 ft on the divide between the White Salmon Glacier and the Price cirque, where the ridge meets the face. Flat bivy ground and a view down onto Price Lake confirm you are there.

Traverse left across the base through the lower glacier's crevasses, keeping climber's right of the main runnel to stay out from under icefall off the Hanging Glacier. Climb the face at about 45 degrees through a notch between rock outcrops near 6,900 ft, steepening to 50 degrees to top out on the shoulder near 8,400 ft. Traverse the plateau around the east side of the pyramid and finish up its central gully.
wa_mount_shuksan_sulphide_glacier: From timberline, follow the broad, rolling crest of Shannon Ridge through meadows and broken timber for about 2 miles to a pass near 5,400 ft, where a north-south ridge is met and the Sulphide Glacier and summit pyramid first come into view. Continue up open slopes and snow onto the toe of the glacier to the lower camp at about 6,200 ft; an upper camp sits near 6,500 ft. There is no reliable water late in the season.

Rope up at camp and climb north up the west side of the Sulphide Glacier over a series of rolling steps; near 7,600 ft the angle eases, so bear north-northeast across the upper glacier to the foot of the summit pyramid at about 8,400-8,500 ft. Cross the moat and climb the central gully on the pyramid's south face, the one with rappel anchors, roughly 600 ft of steep snow or blocky rock to the summit.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier: Walk around the gate and follow the old road past the White Salmon Lodge site for about a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, descend to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the glacier's toe; without it, hold your height through the clearcut and contour, losing elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings, to stay out of the slide alder in the valley bottom.

Rope up and climb the White Salmon Glacier, weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses. The basin below sits under the active Hanging Glacier, whose avalanches can sweep it, so move through early and don't linger.
Continue up the glacier among the outcrops to the foot of Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft, the only abrupt steepening on this side of the mountain.

Climb Winnie's Slide, about 150-200 ft of 40-45 degree snow that can be hard snow or ice late season, onto the Upper Curtis Glacier. Cross the Upper Curtis southward: it starts steep, eases, then loses height to the base of Hell's Highway. Keep the rope tight as crevasses open through the summer.

Climb Hell's Highway, a short chute of steep snow or alpine ice between rock cliffs, watching for a moat where snow meets rock, onto the upper west edge of the Sulphide Glacier. Follow the Sulphide northeast to the foot of the summit pyramid and finish by the central gully on its south face (3rd-4th class) or the West Ridge (4th class).
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier: Reached from the Canadian side: a rough spur off the Chilliwack Lake road leads to a washout near 2,600 ft, then an overgrown roadbed runs to the boundary obelisk and register. Follow the climbers' path up Depot Creek through old growth to the falls, where wet slabs and an old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in, and on to the camp at Ouzel Lake near 5,700 ft. Carry a passport.

From the lake's north side, climb northeast up the obvious wide gully to the Custer-Spickard saddle at 7,380 ft. At the right gap both summits are identifiable and the glacier runs away from the col on the far side.

Step onto the Silver Glacier beyond the saddle and rope up. Climb from about 7,400 ft to where the glacier flattens near 8,300 ft, cross the flat section to the sub-summit notch at about 8,500 ft, then climb the short, loose, lichen-covered Class 4 rock step to the true summit.
wa_mushroom_tower_standard: Rope up and climb low-fifth-class blocky granite up the south side, taking the path of least resistance with gear in the horizontal breaks, to the gap below the summit block.

Make the exposed step across the gap onto the overhanging, mushroom-capped summit block. It is the crux and essentially unprotected, and feels harder when wet or verglassed. The two old bolts on top are the rappel anchor.
wa_mutchler_peak_scramble: Walk the abandoned FR-1570 roadbed past the washed-out culvert, stepping over several windfalls including a large log about 0.8 mile in, to its end at an old clearing with a firepit beside a reliable creek, the last easy water before the ridge.

From the firepit the unmarked climbers' path climbs steeply at once through old-growth forest on exposed roots, with spur tracks around blowdown and stretches where the tread fades, roughly 2,500 ft up to a broad saddle near 4,800 ft north of Found Peak. The path is easy to lose here in fog.

Relocate the boot path at the saddle and follow it up through grass and boulders about 600 ft into a meadow with Found Lake below, then continue south past Found Peak, descending the steep path through the cliffs, and climb over Point 5695 on Kindy Ridge.
Drop south to the next saddle, then leave the ridge and descend west into the Cyclone Lake basin. Rough campsites sit on the benches above the lake, with water from the lake and the tarns above it.
From camp, head south across the basin and ridge terrain toward Mutchler Peak, then climb the heather and blocky rock slopes onto its upper flank. The heather is loose and slick when wet.
Scramble Class 2-3 blocky rock to the summit, with some loose rock near the top.
wa_north_ridge_4: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail about 6 miles to McAllister Camp, then the climbers' trail up the ridge between McAllister and Thunder Creeks to a bivy near 6,000 ft at the Borealis Glacier's toe. Rather than heading for Lucky Pass, circle the glacial lake at the terminus and cross a short stretch of glacier to the foot of the North Ridge, then climb about 1,000 ft of loose blocks, towers and banded low-fifth rock to the summit.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route: Leave the couloir where the hanging glacier sits on your right and take the leftmost of the rock ribs above it, following that rib to the summit. The line is clean rock with no brush; if you find yourself pulling on trees or heather, you are on one of the neighboring ribs, not this one.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse: Follow Hannegan Pass Trail #674 up the Ruth Creek valley about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Hannegan Pass at about 5,066 ft, where the climbers' path leaves the maintained trail.

From the pass, take the faint climbers' path east and south past the pond below the pass, around a cliff-band shoulder, and onto the north slope of the Ruth Glacier. Climb the glacier, which is more crevassed than it looks, to camp at about 6,600 ft by the notch northwest of Ruth's summit.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble: Follow the olivine crest south toward Skookum to Jaws' Tooth, the slender detached spire just north of the summit. Go over the tooth and rappel or downclimb low fifth-class ground to the notch on its south side, then rope up for the exposed crest of the north ridge, about 5.4 on small positive edges, to the summit.
wa_south_face: From the pullout, find the faint boot path dropping east through loose talus into the trees past a trail register, cross Early Winters Creek on a log at about 4,080 ft, and climb the steep timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek to the bivy.
Continue up the climbers' path through loose scree gullies, with snow early in the season, to Burgundy Col at about 7,800 ft. Vasiliki Tower is the formation on your left as you arrive.
wa_south_face_2: From Burgundy Col, do not drop straight toward Pernod's south side. Instead traverse and scramble around the east, Silver Star Creek, side of the ridge below Chianti on loose scree gullies and fourth-class ground; if the ground is still walkable, you have not started the traverse.

Continue the traverse to the notch between Pernod and Chablis at the base of the South Face, carrying a rope for the last moves. Climb two pitches: good cracks through a right-facing corner toward the bunny-ear notch, then a thin-hands splitter that finishes with an aid move off a bolt to the summit (5.9 A0).
wa_sw_couloir_and_face: From the foot of the icefall, climb about 100 ft of snow steepening to 45 degrees to the large transverse crevasse that spans the line, cross it on a snow bridge after testing it, and continue straight into the open-book rock corner, where the ice chimney is the vertical band in its middle.

Above the chimney, climb steep snow to the top of the icefall and an unprotected band of easy fifth-class rock onto the glacier tongue, cross the second crevasse at its left end, and climb 60 to 70 degree ice to the headwall. Traverse left on fourth-class rock and around a corner to the long buttress, follow it to the Southeast Ridge, then drop east onto the Sulphide Glacier and go north to climb the summit pyramid.
wa_the_chopping_block_south_route: From the cairn the climbers' path leaves the roadbed and runs through the woods on the south side of Terror Creek for about a mile to the crossing at roughly 2,000 ft. Cross on the logs if they bridge the creek, or wade a flat stretch nearby; it is about calf-deep by late summer, and it is the last reliable water before high camp.

From the creek, climb the very steep climbers' path almost straight up the side of the ridge, on roots and third-class dirt scrambling, to gain the crest of the Barrier between Terror and Crescent Creeks.

Follow the crest of the Barrier upward through blueberry brush. The path fades in and out and disappears at blowdowns, so stay on the crest to timberline near 5,600 ft and the open, gentle slab and heather basin of Stump Hollow.

From Stump Hollow, climb snow, slabs and heather to the foot of the Chopping Block and the loose gully on its south side that gains the sloping south face. Wear helmets and keep parties out of each other's fall line.

Climb the loose gully and the 200-ft chimney above it, then mixed face and ridge scrambling with some scrubby vegetation and a few low-fifth-class moves below the summit slab. A line kept near the east side of the peak reaches the summit plateau with the least difficulty.
wa_the_devils_club: Take the water taxi about 15 miles up Ross Lake to the Little Beaver dock and follow the Little Beaver Trail west about 5 miles to Perry Creek Camp. Then go trailless south up the Perry Creek drainage, in the creekbed to about 3,600 ft and on the south (true left) bank above it, to the cirque at the toe of the East Face; plan on two days to the base. Climb the face to the summit.
wa_the_exorcism_of_mark_hanna: Head straight uphill from the pullout into the talus below the Supercave gully, take the short forced dogleg out left, and rejoin the gully. Stop at the first, lower ledge system, about an hour up, and walk it to the single belay bolt on a small ledge that marks the start; the broad upper ledge beneath the cave is about ten minutes higher and is too far.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation: Head straight uphill from the pullout into the talus below the Supercave gully, take the short forced dogleg out left, and rejoin the gully. Continue past the lower ledge to the upper ledge at the foot of the wall, about 1 hour 10 minutes from the road; the loose talus steepens near the top. The route shares its start with The Tiger.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route: From the notch, drop into Crescent Creek Basin, cross the glacier below Degenhardt, and climb a loose class 3 gully of rock and dirt to the ridge crest at the col between Degenhardt and The Pyramid, at about 7,500 ft.

From the col, make a few low-fifth-class moves off the ridge crest onto The Pyramid's west side, then scramble the class 3 gully system up and right toward the summit, staying left in the gully to avoid the band of overhanging rock that caps it.
wa_the_west_face: Climb the West Face from the shared start with the Northwest Corner: a dirty chimney to a sandy ledge, a steep right-facing corner, a lieback and undercling pitch, then the thin tips-crack crux, and finish on low-angle cracks with a friction-slab traverse right to the top.
wa_three_fingers_r2: Hike Trail #641 past Saddle Lake at about 2.5 miles and through the Goat Flats meadows at about 4.5 miles to Tin Can Gap, where the maintained tread ends. Drop about 400 ft off-trail onto the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier and cross it, minding the moat and any open crevasses, to the foot of Middle Peak's south face, then scramble solid 3rd and 4th class rock that turns looser 3rd class higher up to the summit.
wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes: From the lake, leave the shore for the broad basin and slopes on the peak's south side rather than the face directly above the water, aiming for the low point on the summit ridge. There are no cairns or path; route-find by the terrain.
Climb the steep grade of loose talus and heather benches toward the low point on the summit ridge. Footing is unstable and there is no tread, so note your line for the descent.

Gain the summit ridge at its low point and finish with a short, exposed class 3 rock scramble to the top. If a continuous snow couloir splits the summit block above you, you have come round onto the north side.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes: Continue up the boot path through forest and then heather to the flat bench at Borealis Lake, the standard base camp below the Borealis Glacier.

Rope up and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle. The glacier is split into a lower and an upper tier by slabs and cliffs; the upper tier leads to Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and Tricouni.

From the col turn east, away from Primus, and climb the single steep snow finger about 200 ft up Tricouni's southwest side, then scramble class 3-4 rock ramps and ledges up the west ridge to the bouldery summit.
wa_west_twin_needle_south_route: Beyond the ford, climb the steep, brushy rib called the Barrier on a faded, easy-to-lose boot path through slide alder and tree debris toward timberline. Water is scarce above about 5,400 ft, so fill up below the Barrier.

From the top of the Barrier drop about 200 ft into Crescent Creek Basin and traverse roughly a mile north across scree to the flat camp below Mount Terror at about 6,050 ft, fed by two streams off the slabs above.
wa_western_dihedral: From the saddle go left (west) about 10 minutes to the base of Skeena26 and scramble about 100 m of class 4 ramps and grooves to a large shelf. Follow it left to a deep gully (a two-bolt anchor allows a hand line or short rappel), cross it, and follow the cairned track west across talus and cedar ribs to the talus field below the far western wall. Climb the reddish right-facing corner five pitches to the top.
wa_whistler_mountain_scramble: Rainy Pass is on SR-20 (North Cascades Highway), about 35 miles west of Winthrop and about 51 miles east of Marblemount. Park in the Pacific Crest Trail North lot on the north side of the pass at about 4,850 ft, beside the Road 600 turnoff. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park, and SR-20 is closed over the pass in winter.

Leave the PCT almost at once and head east cross-country into open forest, climbing steeply through timber and over downed logs with no maintained tread. At about 6,100 ft the trees open into a meadow basin; walk south through it, then turn east and climb the rocky west ridge, staying north of the loose gully, to the band of downsloping slabs and gravelly ledges just below the summit ridge.
Enter the rock gully at the top of the ridge and use the visible ramp along the headwall to reach the summit. Expect loose gravel on downsloping slab; wear a helmet for rockfall from parties above.
wa_wright_pond: There is no trail. From the parking area, walk up through the woods toward the wall, gaining height quickly, then traverse left through open forest and across slabby benches to a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side, about 1 to 1.5 hours from the car.
wa_amphitheater_mountain_finger_of_fatwa: Hike Andrews Creek Trail #504 about 12 miles to Andrews Pass at about 6,700 ft, then descend into the Spanish Creek drainage about 3 miles to the Spanish Camp guard station. Just before the cabin, take the trail on the right about 3 miles up to Upper Cathedral Lake. The route is on Middle Finger, the biggest buttress on the wall directly above the lake, a short walk and scramble from the shore.

Climb the route's four pitches: a rightward ramp and flake, a thin crack and stemming corner to a belay under the roofs, through both roofs into a chimney, then hand cracks and blocky ground trending right onto the rib of the Middle Finger Buttress - Left Side route. Scramble from there to the top of the buttress.
wa_amphitheater_mountain_middle_finger_b: Climb the chimney start into the long hand-crack pitch, traverse right following the continuation of the dihedral, then finish on moderate, non-sustained climbing to the top of the buttress.
Climb the steep slab with its thin vertical crack and the short crux pitch above it, then follow the northwest-facing cracks up the right side of the buttress to its top.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_south_route: From SR 20 at the Mazama turnoff (about 14 miles west of Winthrop), go through Mazama and follow Lost River Road about 7 miles to the end of the pavement, then continue on Harts Pass Road (FR 5400), a narrow, steep, single-lane gravel road with pullouts, about 12 more miles to Harts Pass at about 6,200 ft. Trailers are prohibited. Park where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north. A free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit is required.

Walk north on the Pacific Crest Trail about 27 miles over open high country to Castle Pass, then drop into the head of Castle Creek and out into the open basin below the peak's south side, camping around 5,500 ft. From camp climb the wide south gully to about 6,800 ft, move into the northeast gully to a notch near 7,400 ft, then cross slabs, boulders and snow patches south of the top to a short scramble onto the summit.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble: From SR 20 at the Mazama turnoff (about 14 miles west of Winthrop), turn onto Lost River Road and after half a mile turn left to stay on it. Follow it about 7.5 miles to the end of the pavement, then 1.25 miles on gravel FR 5400 to the Robinson Creek Trailhead on the right, at about 2,500 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park; fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.
wa_mount_ballard_south: Keep following the Mill Creek valley upstream through slide alder and downed timber, losing and refinding the tread, to the old Azurite Mine workings at about 4,400 ft, roughly 11 miles from the trailhead. The flat ground among the workings is the usual first camp.

Leave the trail at the mine and climb steeply east through brush, about 2,000 ft, until the timber gives out in the open basin at roughly 6,600 ft, where the whole south flank of Ballard is visible above you.

Climb the chosen gully, with a few short 3rd and 4th class steps, to the summit block and scramble onto the crest. The northern high point with the old survey mark is the lower one; keep working south along the crest until the ground stops rising at the true summit, 8,371 ft.
wa_mount_carru_scramble: From SR 20 at Mazama follow Lost River Road to the end of the pavement, then the narrow gravel Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) to Harts Pass. At the guard station cabin turn right onto Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600) and climb to the Slate Pass Trailhead at the second switchback beyond the horse loading area, about 6,900 ft. The road is usually open July to September. Fill out the free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk.

Cross Slate Pass and descend the Slate Pass Trail east to the Robinson Creek Trail, then climb the last meadows north to Robinson Pass and drop into the Middle Fork Pasayten valley. Follow the valley trail north, then turn east at the junction where the trail to Fred's Lake and Lake Doris leaves the Middle Fork and climb to the lake, which sits a short way off the main trail.
From the creek, climb back up east into the open meadows and talus of Shellrock Basin, where tarns give water for camp.

From camp head for the scree-and-talus gully that drops south from the Lago-Carru col. Its foot is choked with avalanche debris, so climb the open forest on its west side and step into the bed higher up, then scramble the gully around a couple of short rock steps until the walls fall back at the broad col.

At the col turn left, west, onto Carru's broad southeast ridge and follow any of the parallel scree and talus ribs to the summit, with short class 3 blocks at the top. Stay on the south side of the crest; the north side falls away as a steep cliffed face.
wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face: From SR 20 at the Mazama turnoff (about 14 miles west of Winthrop), turn onto Lost River Road and after half a mile turn left to stay on it. Follow it about 7.5 miles to the end of the pavement, then 1.25 miles on gravel FR 5400 to the Robinson Creek Trailhead on the right, at about 2,500 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park; fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.
wa_north_face_left_buttress: Drive SR 20 east from Marblemount about 28 miles, past Diablo, to the Ross Dam Trailhead pullout between mileposts 134 and 135, at about 2,100 ft. From here a spur trail drops about a mile and 700 ft to Ross Lake near the dam for the water taxi or a carried-in boat. Camping along the Ross Lake corridor needs a park backcountry permit from the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble: From SR 20 at the Mazama junction, cross into Mazama and turn left on Lost River Road (County Road 9140), which becomes Harts Pass Road, FR 5400, where the pavement ends. Follow this narrow road (no trailers) roughly 19 miles to Harts Pass. At the guard station turn right on the Slate Peak road, FR 5400-600, and park at its second switchback below the gated road end, near 6,900 ft. A free self-issued Pasayten Wilderness permit is required.

Take the Slate Pass Trail as it drops steeply through larch and meadows, losing about 1,500 ft, to the Middle Fork Pasayten (Robinson Creek) Trail #478. Turn north and follow it downstream along the river, fording several side creeks that can run high early in the season and working through heavy blowdown, to the Berk Creek Trail junction.

Gain the ridge crest north of camp and follow open tundra and talus north along the ridge, keeping to the climbers' path on the west side of Points 8207 and 8165, with a short exposed step or two near the rock points south of Dot Mountain. Continue over or around Dot to the meadow saddle between Dot and Ptarmigan, which holds a small tarn at about 7,800 ft.
From the tarn basin, scramble a short way north over talus onto the crest of Ptarmigan's south ridge.

Walk north up the broad, rounded south ridge on Class 2 tundra and talus, with a few short rock steps near the top, to the summit. Keep to the gentle slopes; the north face drops away sheer just beyond the summit.
wa_remmel_mountain_southeast_slope: From SR 20 in Winthrop, take East Chewuch Road north about 7 miles and turn right onto FR 51. Continue north up the Chewuch valley, staying on the road as it becomes FR 5160, to its end at the Thirtymile Trailhead, about 3,400 ft, where the Chewuch River Trail #510 begins. A free self-issued Pasayten Wilderness permit is required.
From the cairn, follow the well-trodden unofficial path west up open meadow and talus to the summit.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet: Start at the lowest point of the south face and climb five pitches straight up the middle of the face on natural gear, passing the big mid-face roof on its left side, to the top of the tower.
wa_the_monk_odine: Climb the prominent crack line left of center on the south face: two pitches up a chimney and then a dirty, vegetated gully with loose rock, followed by the superb 4-inch splitter jam crack, to the top of the tower.
wa_the_monk_scabo: From the large ledge near the right-hand side of the lowest part of the south face, climb five pitches that wander back and forth up the right side of the face to the top of the tower. Extend placements to keep the rope running straight.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble: From the mine camp junction, follow Boundary Trail #533 west for about a mile, climbing gently to around 6,900 ft, to the point where the trail stops running along the mountain's flank and turns south toward Apex Pass. If the trail is heading south and climbing away from the mountain, you have passed the bend.

Leave the trail at the bend and climb straight up the broad, gentle west slope of heather and talus, Class 2 with no cliff band, heading east and northeast to the summit. Lines farther round to the north or south break into short low Class 3 steps and are not the way to go.
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier: At Anderson Pass leave the maintained trail and follow the unsigned climbers' path north up the moraine to the snowy saddle above the small tarn at about 5,100 ft. Traverse above the tarn, not around it at its level, and climb the single steep snow finger from its far side, 40 degrees or more in its steepest section, to the notch of Flypaper Pass between Mount Anderson and Echo Rock.

From Flypaper Pass drop about 200 ft onto the Eel Glacier, getting around the bergschrund below the headwall, and traverse north around the rock buttress. Climb east on the upper glacier to the saddle north of the summit at about 7,200 ft, then scramble the last loose, exposed rock and snow patches to the top.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble: From the High Divide follow the trail east toward Cat Peak until the maintained tread ends, then continue on the beaten sidehill track to the start of the Catwalk. Watch for the track that turns uphill onto the ridge; the lower path dead-ends at rocks and leaves only an exposed scramble back up to the crest.

Follow the Catwalk crest to its end at a small flat spot, then climb onto the flanks of Mount Carrie and follow the beaten track on a long sidehill traverse past Eleven Bull Basin, the next good water. The way then drops into the lake basins below the range and climbs on into the open meadows of Upper Ferry Basin below Mount Ferry.

From Bear Pass drop into the flat meadow below and cross it, then contour southeast over scree and lingering snow patches until you are southwest of the summit. There a boot track curls left, to the north, up a moderate scree slope and through one brief patch of brush to the Class 2 summit. The ridge running east off Bear Pass is not the way.
wa_mount_cameron_standard: From Cameron Pass leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up on Class 1-2 scree and talus. The ridge crosses many false summits, so do not stop at the first high point; the true top is still easy ground, and Class 3-4 steps mean you have passed it and started the traverse toward the Middle Peak.
wa_mount_clark_standard: Cross the Surprise Basin snowfields and climb talus and scree west-northwest to Surprise Col at about 6,900 ft, the low saddle between Mount Johnson and Mount Clark. Standing in it, Johnson is on your left and Clark's summit tower on your right; the corkscrew starts here.

Walk up talus to the cliffs and skirt right on a wide, easy ledge until a Y-shaped gully opens above; climb it to a boulder, then go right to a notch on the southeast ridge. Descend a diagonal crack to the east ledge (note the cairn at its top for the return), follow it north about 50 yards, climb a loose gully and the Class 4 dihedral ramp (or the Class 3 face on its left), then a slot through the summit block's north face.
wa_mount_hopper_standard: From US 101 at Hoodsport, turn west onto SR 119 (Lake Cushman Road) and drive just over 9 miles to its T-junction with FR 24, then turn left. The pavement ends after 1.7 miles; continue 3.7 miles on gravel to a junction, turn right, and drive 1.2 miles to the Staircase Ranger Station, with trailhead parking across from the campground. An Olympic National Park entrance fee applies.

Follow the North Fork Skokomish River Trail up the valley through old-growth forest, staying on the river trail where the Flapjack Lakes Trail branches off at about 3.7 miles, and continue past Big Log Camp to Camp Pleasant.
Continue up the valley on the North Fork Skokomish River Trail, crossing Eight Stream on a bridge, to Nine Stream Camp, the last reliable camp and water before the trail turns steeply uphill.
Above Nine Stream the trail leaves the valley floor and climbs steeply, about 2,600 ft in 3 miles, past Two Bear Camp and through brush to the saddle of First Divide at 4,688 ft.

The long-abandoned Mount Hopper Way leaves the trail at First Divide, but its tread is lost under brush, so navigate rather than follow: work south and then east through forest and brush toward the open meadows below the peak.

Break out into open subalpine meadow and climb talus to the rockwall below the summit. Several gullies and ribs look alike; take the one that keeps laying back into short climbable steps, note a feature at its foot for the way down, and pick your line early on the narrow, loose summit crest.
wa_mount_la_crosse_scramble: Fill water at the river, then turn north onto the La Crosse Pass Trail and climb about 3 miles and 2,900 ft of steep, eroded switchbacks to the bald, waterless saddle of La Crosse Pass at 5,566 ft.

Leave the trail at the top of the pass and follow the broad ridge crest west over heather benches and then talus to the summit, Class 2 with brief Class 3 near the top. White Mountain, to the southwest, is the more obvious summit from the pass; keep to the ridge leading west, and take a bearing off the saddle before leaving it.
wa_mount_lawson_standard: From the ford, climb off-trail up Lawson's north side through steep, unmarked timber and into the long gully system that leads toward the North Ridge, on loose scree or firm snow depending on season.
Climb out the top of the gully onto the North Ridge and follow it to the broad summit plateau.
wa_mount_mystery_standard: Get onto the Mystery Glacier at its lower left corner and cross it diagonally, trending right, to the col at about 6,700 ft on the peak's east side. From the col traverse mixed rock and snow to open snow about 200 ft south, climb it staying south of the blocky rock band, and continue up loose rock to the notch, trending climber's left as you approach it.
From the notch, climb the gully to the summit block; the rock improves markedly near the top.
wa_mount_seattle_south: From Low Divide, follow the Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail west, climbing across the lower slopes of Mount Seattle about 1,000 ft to Seattle Meadows, the meadow camp in upper Seattle Basin at about 4,550 ft on the peak's southern flank.

From camp, walk up through the meadows of Upper Seattle Basin and climb scree on the peak's western side, cross over the connecting ridge, then continue up scree and talus on the eastern side. A Class 2-3 scramble up the east ridge reaches the craggy summit, where the register is kept in a large plastic tube jammed in a crack.
wa_mount_steel_standard: Follow Duckabush River Trail #803 up the valley. At about 3.9 miles it climbs roughly 1,000 ft of steep, loose switchbacks over Big Hump, then drops back to the river; continue past Five Mile Camp, into Olympic National Park at about 6.2 miles, and on through old growth and burned forest to Ten-Mile Camp.
Continue up the Duckabush River Trail through the upper valley, about 7 miles, to Upper Duckabush Camp, the last camp on the river, where the trail from First Divide comes in.

Above camp the trail fords the Duckabush, a wide crossing that can run thigh-deep and swift in early season or after rain; scout for the best braid and use a pole. Continue up the trail toward Marmot Lake to the start of the steep final climb.
Climb the final steep mile on loose, eroded tread to Marmot Lake at about 4,400 ft.

From camp, drop back down the trail to where an unmarked feeder creek comes in from the south (no sign, cairns at best), and follow the creek up into the rocky amphitheater on the west side of Mount Steel's summit. Fill water at the creek; it is scarce above.

From the amphitheater, climb easy Class 2 heather benches and talus, snow-covered into July, to the summit ridge and the 6,225 ft high point. Carry an ice axe early in the season and stay back from cornices on the ridge, which linger into late June.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble: Follow the Elwha River Trail south up the valley through old-growth forest, past the Humes Ranch cutoff and the Lillian River crossing, to Mary's Falls Camp, about 8.8 miles from Whiskey Bend.
Continue up the Elwha River Trail past Canyon Camp and Elkhorn to the Hayes River Guard Station, about 16 miles from Whiskey Bend.
Continue up the Elwha River Trail about 3.7 miles beyond Hayes River to Camp Wilder in the river bottom east of the peak.

Fill water, then leave the maintained trail at Camp Wilder and climb cross-country, first through streamside brush and old forest, to the open heather benches and headwater creeks below Mount Wilder's south face. There is no path or cairned line.
Above the benches, climb the loose scree and talus of the south face toward the south ridge, keeping the party close together because of rockfall.
Gain the south ridge and follow it at Class 2 to the summit.
wa_sundial_northeast: Follow the Upper Dungeness Trail about 1 mile along the river, cross Royal Creek on a footlog bridge and turn right onto the Royal Basin Trail, staying left at the Maynard Burn Trail junction. The trail switchbacks up the Royal Creek valley, crossing the creek on log bridges.

Continue up the Royal Basin Trail into Olympic National Park, across open talus stretches with views up the valley, back to the creek past campsites, and up switchbacks on open slopes to Royal Lake at about 5,100 ft, 7.2 miles from the trailhead.
Continue up-valley past the lake on the trail toward Upper Royal Basin; Shelter Rock is the massive overhanging boulder on the left.
Beyond Shelter Rock, cross a footlog and climb steeply until the trail levels out into Arrowhead Meadow.
Cross an unbridged stream and make the final climb into Upper Royal Basin at about 5,700 ft, where milky-blue tarns lie to the west, about 8 miles from the trailhead.

From the tarns, look up at the Needles and pick out the northeast-facing gully on the climber's-right side of the group, the obvious white line when it still holds snow. Cross the talus to its foot, where the scree fan narrows and steepens, and climb into the gully; an axe and crampons help while it holds snow, into July.

Climb the gully to where it doglegs left below a notch on the summit ridge. From the notch, a short, exposed Class 3 scramble leads south to the true summit; where the ledges appear to cliff out, a cairned crack around the corner is the way through.
wa_the_horn_scramble: Follow the North Fork Skokomish River Trail, an old roadbed on a gentle grade, about 3.4 miles up the valley to the Flapjack Lakes Trail junction at Spike Camp.
Take the Flapjack Lakes Trail and climb steeply beside Madeline Creek and its small waterfalls to the junction with the Black and White Lakes Trail, about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes.
Continue up the Flapjack Lakes Trail, steeper now, about half a mile to Flapjack Lakes.
From the lakes, follow the Gladys Divide trail east to about 4,400 ft and leave the tread just before a small pond.
From the notch, climb the Southeast or Southwest Route, a single run-out 5.5 pitch of steep pillow basalt, to the summit. Two ropes are wanted for the rappel back into the notch.
adams_northwest_ridge: From camp, get onto the north-facing slope between the Adams Glacier and the crest of the Northwest Ridge, gaining it below the glacier's terminus to stay clear of its crevasses and moats. Steepening 40 to 45 degree neve leads through a single narrow pinch in a rock band to the ridge crest near 10,000 ft; stay off the loose crest below that point, then continue up the ridge to the summit.
rainier_central_mowich_face: There is no public road to Mowich Lake: SR 165 is closed at the Fairfax Bridge south of Carbonado to vehicles, bicycles and walkers, with no detour. The lake can only be reached on foot along the Wonderland Trail from another part of the park, a multi-day walk; camping on the way needs a park wilderness permit.
rainier_north_mowich_headwall: There is no public road to Mowich Lake: SR 165 is closed at the Fairfax Bridge south of Carbonado to vehicles, bicycles and walkers, with no detour. The lake can only be reached on foot along the Wonderland Trail from another part of the park, a multi-day walk; camping on the way needs a park wilderness permit.
wa_gilbert_peak_conrad_glacier: From US 12 at Rimrock Lake east of White Pass, take Tieton Road (FS Road 1200) to South Fork Tieton Road (FS Road 1000) and follow it about 12.6 miles, paved then good gravel, to the road end at Conrad Meadows, about 4,000 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is required to park, and a free Goat Rocks Wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead.

Walk the road a quarter mile to the gate and take South Fork Tieton Trail #1120 about 4.5 miles to the loop junction; go right (north) about 2 miles, then near 5,100 ft turn right up an unmarked pack trail to a ridge crest and on west and north through benches to a Conrad Creek waterfall at 6,000 ft. Pass Barren Lake, climb the east side of the Conrad Glacier to the 7,200 ft saddle, traverse the Meade Glacier west-southwest to the south ridge and scramble it to the summit.
wa_gilbert_peak_west_route: From Packwood, drive US 12 west about 2.7 miles and turn left (south) on FS Road 21. Follow the gravel road about 13 miles, bear left onto FS Road 2150 toward Chambers Lake, and in under 3 miles turn right to the Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (Trail #96) at about 4,650 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is required, and a free Goat Rocks Wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead.
wa_lane_peak_r1: Walk Stevens Canyon Road west about half a mile to its 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. Stay low into the basin under Lane Peak's north face rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, cross the debris apron, and from its top angle left into the Zipper, the middle of three couloirs: about 1,000 ft of 40 to 45 degree snow with short steps to a dead tree at a notch in the east ridge.
wa_lane_peak_r2: Walk the road a short way, then drop south into the basin toward Tatoosh Creek and climb the debris triangle to the base of the north-face couloirs, about 45 to 75 minutes. The Fly is the rightmost and broadest of the three, 40 to 50 ft wide; climb it at about 45 degrees, trending slightly right, as it eases to 30 to 35 degrees near its top at the notch in the west ridge.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder: Follow the Wonderland Trail south up the Fryingpan Creek valley through old-growth forest to the crossing of Fryingpan Creek at about 3.2 miles and roughly 1,400 ft of gain. Take care here in high runoff.

Beyond the crossing the trail switchbacks up out of the forest to the subalpine meadows of Summerland at about 4.5 miles and 5,900 ft, with its stone shelter, toilet and the last reliable running water.

Leave the Wonderland Trail on the climbers' path and climb steep tundra and the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop near 7,400 ft with flat bivy sites. Stay on the cairned line left of the bowl under the rock bands; contouring right into it cliffs you out. Above Meany Crest a steep slope of about 300 ft gains the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier.

Rope up and climb south and southwest across the gentler slopes of the Fryingpan Glacier to Whitman Notch at about 9,100 ft, the low point in Whitman Crest where the Whitman Glacier first comes into view. Crevasses open on the Fryingpan as the season goes on.

Cross onto the Whitman Glacier and traverse its upper part at low angle to get past the cliffs, then turn uphill on steepening snow to the bergschrund below the summit pyramid, probing for hidden crevasses.

Step over the bergschrund and climb snow of 45 degrees or more to where the glacier ends near 10,500 ft in a steep gully of loose rock and scree. Continue up the gully, a steep snowfield below a cliff band and one more rocky gully onto the high shoulder. Wear helmets and keep out of each other's fall line.

Scramble across a tiny notch and up the final face, Class 3 to 4 on rotten andesite, then along the narrow crest to the summit at 11,138 ft. Many parties rope up; the crest drops about 2,000 ft to the Emmons Glacier on the north side.
wa_mount_adams_north_ridge: Head southeast from High Camp onto the foot of the North Ridge, which is gained almost right away above camp without crossing a glacier. Early in the season snow can hide the path, so carry a compass.

Scramble about 2,500 ft up the crest on loose rock, scree and pumice, mostly Class 2 with some Class 3, staying on the crest where you can and occasionally dropping to the west side around obstacles. From about 10,000 ft snowfields lead on, including one steep section with no runout above the Lava Glacier, to the ice cap near 12,000 ft; then walk about a mile across the summit plateau to the summit.
wa_mount_rainier_emmons_glacier: Leave Camp Schurman straight up the Emmons Glacier to Emmons Flats, a level bench just above Steamboat Prow. Continue up toward the crater rim, weaving around crevasses, until a snow ramp lets you move left near 10,200 ft onto the Corridor, a smooth rib of snow running up the fall line to roughly 11,600 ft.

Where crevasses and seracs block the direct line at the top of the Corridor, angle climber's right into the broad apron below the saddle between Liberty Cap and the crater, switchbacking around crevasses to a ramp across the final bergschrund near 13,000 ft. Gain the crater rim and traverse to Columbia Crest. The line changes through the season, so keep a GPS track for the descent.
wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face: Follow the Wonderland Trail about 0.3 mile to the Spray Park Trail and climb it through Spray Park past Spray Falls. Where it tops out, go cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock onto Ptarmigan Ridge, leave the ridge near 8,300 ft and drop about 1,000 ft to the North Mowich Glacier, and rope up to the camps at 9,600 to 10,200 ft. Turn the bergschrund, climb the face to the bench near 13,300 ft, and continue to Liberty Cap.
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge: From Ashford, follow SR 706 east to the Nisqually Entrance of Mount Rainier National Park. About 1 mile past the entrance, turn left onto Westside Road and follow the gravel road about 3 miles to the barricade at Dry Creek, where it closes to vehicles; park in the small lot south of it. The road to Dry Creek is open to vehicles only in summer, typically May to November, and a park entrance pass is required.
wa_mount_rainier_tahoma_glacier: From Ashford, follow SR 706 east to the park's Nisqually Entrance; a park entrance pass is required. About 1 mile past the entrance, turn left onto Westside Road and drive about 3 miles to the gate at the Dry Creek trailhead, near 2,900 ft, and park below the barricade. The road beyond is closed to vehicles, and the drivable section is open only in the summer season.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1: Follow Trail 96 up through forest, crossing Goat Creek on a footbridge at about 1.9 miles and passing the springs at the head of Snowgrass Creek, then ford Snowgrass Creek on logs and rocks. At about 3.9 miles the Bypass Trail 97 forks right toward Cispus Basin; stay left on Trail 96.
Stay on Trail 96 as it breaks out of the forest into the open heather meadows and wildflower bogs of Snowgrass Flat at about 5,800 ft.
Continue up Trail 96 through the meadows, going straight past the Trail 86 junction (left, to Goat Lake), and climb in long open benches to meet the Pacific Crest Trail at about 6,400 ft.

Turn left (north) on the PCT and follow it about 1.6 to 1.8 miles across the rocky, increasingly exposed west flank of Old Snowy, where snow can linger into midsummer. Watch for the unmarked climbers' path, the first thing that turns uphill, branching right (east) toward a rocky saddle on the northwest ridge. If the PCT starts descending, you have passed it.
Take the climbers' path right off the PCT and switchback steeply uphill toward the northwest ridge until the tread gives way to loose scree and talus.
Scramble the last few hundred feet over loose Class 2-3 rock and talus to the summit, staying out of the fall line of parties above.
wa_scramble_route: From the saddle where the maintained trail ends, follow the climbers' path along the narrow, exposed ridge for about a quarter mile of scrambling. Below the loose Class 4 rock step, go left 100 to 200 ft into a short Class 3 gully, climb it to a ledge and rejoin the line above the step. Higher, the false summit sits on the left; stay right for the true summit.
